{{Short description|Concept in metric geometry}}
In [[metric geometry]], the '''metric tangent cone''' of a [[metric space]] is a generalization of the [[tangent space]] from [[Riemannian geometry]]. It is obtained as a local blow up of the metric space at a point, taken using [[Gromov–Hausdorff convergence]]. It is also called a '''Gromov tangent cone''', or simply a '''tangent cone''' when the metric setting is clear.<ref name="Gromov2007">{{cite book |last=Gromov |first=Mikhail |author-link=Mikhail Gromov (mathematician) |title=Metric Structures for Riemannian and Non-Riemannian Spaces |series=Modern Birkhäuser Classics |publisher=Birkhäuser Boston |year=2007 |orig-year=1999 |isbn=978-0-8176-4582-3 |doi=10.1007/978-0-8176-4583-0}}</ref><ref name="BBI2001">{{cite book |last1=Burago |first1=Dmitri |last2=Burago |first2=Yuri |last3=Ivanov |first3=Sergei |title=A Course in Metric Geometry |series=Graduate Studies in Mathematics |volume=33 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |location=Providence, Rhode Island |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-8218-2129-9}}</ref> It is related to the notion of a [[tangent cone]]: for a Riemannian manifold with singularities, for example, it is the ordinary tangent cone.

== Definition ==

Let <math>(X,d)</math> be a metric space and let <math>x\in X</math>. A pointed metric space <math>(Y,d_Y,o)</math> is called a '''metric tangent space''' of <math>X</math> at <math>x</math> if there is a sequence of positive numbers <math>r_i\to 0</math> such that
<math display="block">
(X,r_i^{-1}d,x)\to (Y,d_Y,o)
</math>
in the pointed Gromov–Hausdorff topology.<ref name="BBI2001" /> The base point <math>o</math> is the image, in the limiting space, of the point about which the original space is blown up.

== Properties ==
A Gromov tangent space records the first-order metric geometry of a space at a point. It is invariant under local isometry and under uniform rescaling of the original metric. If a tangent space is unique, then rescaling the tangent space again gives an isometric tangent space, so uniqueness implies a form of metric self-similarity. The word "cone" denotes this self-similarity under dilations.

Existence is not automatic for arbitrary metric spaces. It is usually obtained from compactness theorems, such as Gromov compactness, together with local hypotheses such as properness, local compactness, doubling estimates, or curvature bounds.<ref name="Gromov2007" /><ref name="BBI2001" /> Even when tangent spaces exist, they may depend on the sequence <math>r_i\to0</math>.

== Examples ==

=== Euclidean and Riemannian spaces ===

For <math>\mathbb R^n</math> with its Euclidean metric, the Gromov tangent space at every point is again <math>\mathbb R^n</math>. This is because the rescaled metric space is already isometric with the original Euclidean space. More generally, if <math>M</math> is a smooth <math>n</math>-dimensional Riemannian manifold, then the Gromov tangent space at <math>p\in M</math> is the ordinary tangent vector space <math>T_pM</math> equipped with the Euclidean norm induced by the Riemannian metric.<ref name="Gromov2007" /><ref name="BBI2001" />

For spaces with boundary or singularities, the tangent space may cease to be a vector space. For example, the metric tangent at a smooth boundary point of a Riemannian manifold with boundary is modeled on a Euclidean half-space.

=== Sub-Riemannian geometry ===

In [[sub-Riemannian geometry]], Gromov tangent spaces are typically non-Euclidean. At a regular point of a sub-Riemannian manifold, [[Mitchell's theorem]] identifies the pointed Gromov–Hausdorff tangent cone with a nilpotent approximation of the bracket-generating distribution, equipped with its [[Carnot–Carathéodory metric]]. In particular, the tangent object is a [[Carnot group]] in the equiregular case.<ref name="Mitchell1985">{{cite journal |last=Mitchell |first=John |title=On Carnot-Carathéodory metrics |journal=Journal of Differential Geometry |volume=21 |issue=1 |year=1985 |pages=35–45 |doi=10.4310/jdg/1214439462}}</ref><ref name="Bellaiche1996">{{cite book |last=Bellaïche |first=André |chapter=The tangent space in sub-Riemannian geometry |editor1-last=Bellaïche |editor1-first=André |editor2-last=Risler |editor2-first=Jean-Jacques |title=Sub-Riemannian Geometry |series=Progress in Mathematics |volume=144 |publisher=Birkhäuser Basel |year=1996 |pages=1–78 |isbn=978-3-0348-9946-8 |doi=10.1007/978-3-0348-9210-0_1}}</ref> Carnot groups thus serve as infinitesimal model spaces in sub-Riemannian analysis, replacing the Euclidean spaces that are the infinitesimal models of Riemannian geometry.
